examples: I studied really hard. And yet I failed the exam.
It was raining. And yet he didn't have an umbrella.
She promised. And yet she didn't come.
This shop is popular. And yet there are few customers today.
I told you that you could do it if you tried. And yet you slacked off, didn't you?
fields.explain:
Position: Always at the beginning of the second clause, after a period or comma.
Used when you want to emphasize an emotion: disappointment, indignation, reproach, surprise.
It is not simply a result like それで, nor just “even so” like それでも; it means “it should have been different, but…”.
Often used in spoken language, conversation, or emotional narrative writing.

•
Expresses strong contrast with expectations: Clause B goes completely against what should have followed from clause A.

•
Clear emotional nuance: Usually carries feelings of reproach, surprise, disappointment, or resentment.

•
Natural translations: “And yet…”, “But…”, “Even so…”.

• Difference from それでも: それなのに emphasizes stronger emotion and a clearer contrast.
fields.notes:
• Common in everyday conversation, anime and manga when a character expresses emotion.
• Works well in narrative writing when you want to emphasize the conflict between expectation and reality.
• Often translated as “And yet…”, “But…”, “Even so…”. meaning_vi: But, and yet ～ ⏐ explain: Expresses an unexpected result. ⏐ examples: 1. この時計は高かった。それなのにすぐに壊れた。
This watch was expensive. And yet it broke right away.
2. 一生懸命勉強している。それなのに成績はよくならない。
I'm studying hard. And yet my grades aren't improving.
mistakes: Confusing it with それでも: それでも = “even so, still…”, while それなのに = “and yet…” (emphasizes disappointment).
Using it when the two sentences have no contrasting relationship is incorrect.
Using it in very formal writing is inappropriate; replace it with しかしながら or とはいえ.
Omitting the comma in written language → it should be written “それなのに、…”。

rows: <ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>した。 それなのに<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けた。
Acknowledges A, then B still happens (less emotional).
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。 それでも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Colloquial; no emphasis on emotion or strong contrast.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。 でも<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい。
A result completely contrary to expectation, with a feeling of “oh no!”.
<ruby>勝<rt>か</rt></ruby>つと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った。 ところが<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けた。

examples: Participation is free. However, advance registration is required.
Smoking permitted. However, only in designated areas.
The contract will be renewed automatically. However, it may be changed by agreement of both parties.
We will apply the student discount. However, you must present your student ID.
This medicine is for adults. However, pregnant women should consult a doctor.
fields.explain:
Always at the beginning of the sentence that follows, followed by a comma: “ただし、…”.
Suitable for setting the scope/conditions of application, not for emotional argument.
In company documents, なお adds information, while ただし sets a condition/exception.

• Establishes an exception/additional condition that restricts the previous sentence.
• Highly prescriptive; stiffer and more formal in nuance than ただ or でも.
• S2 often contains conditional wording: ～に限る／～を除く／～場合は／要～／原則として…など.
fields.notes:
• “ただし書き” is the “hedging” clause in regulations; it usually follows a declarative main clause.
• In polite emails you can use: ただし、〜となります／〜が必要となります。
• When S2 is a safety warning, ただし helps the reader notice its importance immediately.
mistakes: Using ただし for contrasting personal opinions → unnatural; use しかし/でも/ただ instead.
S2 lacks a prescriptive element (no condition/limitation) → wrong choice in reading questions.
Confusing なお with ただし: なお only adds information and imposes no restriction.
JLPT questions often set the trap “無料。なお、事前登録が必要だ。” → the nuance is not quite right; the answer is usually ただし.

rows: <ruby>無料<rt>むりょう</rt></ruby>。ただし、<ruby>会員<rt>かいいん</rt></ruby>のみ。
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>だ。ただ、<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby><ruby>多数<rt>たすう</rt></ruby>。しかし、<ruby>不満<rt>ふまん</rt></ruby>もある。
<ruby>受付<rt>うけつけ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>9時<rt>きゅうじ</rt></ruby>。なお、<ruby>土日<rt>どにち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>み。
<ruby>祝日<rt>しゅくじつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>除<rt>のぞ</rt></ruby>く<ruby>平日<rt>へいじつ</rt></ruby>

examples: This plan is cheap. The only thing is, the data allowance is small.
You don't need to come to work tomorrow. Just make sure to submit the report in the morning, though.
This medicine works well. However, it can make you drowsy.
The forecast says it will be sunny today. However, the wind is apparently going to get stronger in the afternoon.
This book is easy to read. The only thing is, it has a lot of technical terms.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of the sentence that follows, followed by a comma: “ただ、…”.
S2 is usually an additional condition, an exception, or a safety note.
Neutral and moderately polite; can be used in everyday work emails.
Avoid using ただ for rigid regulations/legal clauses (use ただし in that case).

• Restrictive addition: S2 states a condition, exception, drawback, or note regarding the information in S1.
• Strength: softer than しかし, more neutral than でも; not as formal as ただし.
• Nuance: “S1 is true, it's just that / however S2”. It does not negate S1 but adjusts expectations.
• Context: usable in both spoken and written language; suitable for explanations, negotiations, and stating accompanying conditions.
fields.notes:
• In presentations, ただ helps “soften the blow” when bringing up a drawback after praise.
• Placing ただ between two short sentences saves words compared with けれども/とはいえ while still sounding natural.
• Do not confuse it with ただ = “only/just”: ただ一つ (only one), ただの冗談 (just a joke).
mistakes: Confusing ただ with ただし: questions about regulations/clauses call for ただし, not ただ.
Missing comma after ただ: it should be written “ただ、…”.
Rigid machine-like translation as “however” in every context: for mild requests, translate as “it's just that / but”.
Choosing しかし when a strong counterargument is needed; ただ is a milder level.

rows: Soft; fine in both spoken and written language
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。ただ、<ruby>質<rt>しつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>普通<rt>ふつう</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby><ruby>多数<rt>たすう</rt></ruby>。しかし、<ruby>課題<rt>かだい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>残<rt>のこ</rt></ruby>る。
Strongly colloquial, rarely used in serious writing
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。でも、<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。
Used for regulations and formal conditions
<ruby>無料<rt>むりょう</rt></ruby>。ただし、<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>る。
Written language; concession followed by a counterpoint
<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>だ。とはいえ、<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。

examples: We cut expenses. But the deficit has not been eliminated.
He is young. But he has a wealth of experience.
I ran as fast as I could. But I couldn't catch up.
The proposal is innovative. But it lacks feasibility.
The rain has stopped. But the road surface is still slippery.
fields.explain:
Used to move on to a clearly contrasting clause, keeping the style strong and concise.
Suits narration, argument, and exposition. In polite conversation, しかし/でも/けれども are usually used.
Can stand at the beginning of a paragraph/beginning of a sentence to create a decisive rhythm.

• Meaning: “But/However”. A logical contrastive link, with a written-language, decisive nuance.
• Nuance: masculine, strongly assertive; often seen in essays, expository texts, and journalistic/narrative style.
• Neutrality: less emotional than それなのに; more forceful than しかし in tone (not necessarily in logic).
fields.notes:
• だが is an independent conjunction, different from “〜だ + が” (copula + contrastive particle) within a sentence. Although they look the same, their functions differ.
• In advertising/entertainment style, “だがしかし” is used for exaggeration and rhythm.
• Using だが many times in a row can make the text stiff; alternate it with しかし/一方/ところが depending on the argument. explain: A stiff way of saying　「しかし」　「けれども」. ⏐ examples: 1. これは難しい挑戦だ。だが失敗を恐れてはいけない。
This is a difficult challenge. But we must not be afraid of failure.
2. 生活は貧しい。だが幸せだ。
Life is poor. But I'm happy.
mistakes: Confusing the conjunction “だが” with “〜だ + が” within one sentence: questions may set a trap about sentence-component analysis. A period before だが signals that it is a conjunction.
Using だが in polite conversation with customers → sounds rough; choose しかし/けれども.
Using だが for a concessive “still do it” relationship → off in nuance (use それでも instead).

rows: Neutral and more general; less “sharp” than だが
<ruby>急<rt>いそい</rt></ruby>いだ。しかし<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わず。
Implies resentment/surprise; だが is more neutral
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>。それなのに<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ない。
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いけれども<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>。

examples: The meeting starts at 10. By the way, it will be held in Meeting Room 3.
This restaurant has a good reputation. Incidentally, the owner is a former professional athlete.
This software is free. By the way, there is also a paid version.
He is from Osaka. Incidentally, he doesn't have much of an accent.
I'm on a business trip next week. By the way, I'll be working from home on Friday.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence (a new one), followed by a comma: “ちなみに、…”.
It gives additional information, not a “condition/exception” and not a “conclusion”.
In formal writing, なお replaces ちなみに when a stiffer style is wanted.

• “By the way / incidentally”: provides useful side information that does not determine the main flow.
• Keeps the connection to the topic; it should not change the topic abruptly like ところで.
• Often used in presentations, emails and conversation to insert an interesting/related fact.
fields.notes:
• Use ちなみに to slip in a “fun fact” and make a talk lively, but don't overuse it and dilute the main flow.
• In polite emails: “ちなみにですが、〜をご存じでしょうか。” opens a topic gently.
• If the added information is a condition/exception, switch to ただし/なお for the right nuance. explain: Used to add a small piece of information to the previous sentence (a). ⏐ examples: 1. 最近は、ペットを飼う家が増えているようです。ちなみに、うちにも犬が１ 匹とネコが２ 匹います。
It seems that more and more households have pets these days. By the way, we have one dog and two cats at our house too.
2. 燃えるゴミは月曜日と木曜日、燃えないゴミは金曜日に出してください。ちなみに資源ごみの収集日は第３水曜日です。
Please put out burnable garbage on Mondays and Thursdays and non-burnable garbage on Fridays. By the way, recyclables are collected on the third Wednesday of the month.
mistakes: Using ちなみに to introduce a binding condition → wrong function; ただし must be used.
Confusing it with ところで: questions testing the topic usually require ところで for a sharp shift.
Inserting ちなみに too often confuses the flow; in writing, the answer is sometimes なお (more formal).

rows: Does not change the topic abruptly
<ruby>締切<rt>しめきり</rt></ruby>は<ruby>金曜<rt>きんよう</rt></ruby>。ちなみに、<ruby>土曜<rt>どよう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>み。
Switches to a new topic, changes direction
ところで、<ruby>週末<rt>しゅうまつ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>は？
While doing A, also do B
<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>ついでに<ruby>切符<rt>きっぷ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>受付<rt>うけつけ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>9時<rt>きゅうじ</rt></ruby>。なお、<ruby>午後<rt>ごご</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休止<rt>きゅうし</rt></ruby>。

examples: We are temporarily closed today. Please note that we will open as usual tomorrow.
Applications are accepted online only. Please note that applications cannot be submitted by mail.
The participation fee is 1,000 yen. Note that it is free for students.
I have attached the materials. For details, please refer to page 3.
Reception until 5 p.m. Closed on Saturdays and Sundays.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of the sentence in B; always followed by a comma to separate the content.
Neutral-to-formal tone; suited to official documents, rarely used in casual conversation (replaced by それで/それから/あと).
When it means a “mild exception”, it is weaker than ただし and lacks the strong counterargument nuance of しかし.
Often used with instructional verbs: ご確認ください／ご注意ください／お問い合わせください.

• Adding information: Adds related details, often important to the reader.
• Note/reminder: Shifts to a tone of instruction, warning, or additional rules.
• Correction/exception: States a special case without negating the previous content.
• Nuance: Formal; typical of announcements, administrative documents, manuals, and work emails.
fields.notes:
• In headings/signs, the subject and particles can be omitted: なお、入場は一方通行.
• The kanji 尚 is often used in formal writing; on computers/forms you may see it written entirely in kanji.
• In emails, “なお” often comes right before a sentence containing a keigo verb requesting an action. explain: Used when adding something to the conversation. It does not necessarily have to be related to the previous sentence.
2
「今日はこれで終わります。 なお 次回の日時は・・・」 We'll finish here for today. In addition, the date and time of the next session is…
mistakes: Using なお in casual conversation → sounds stiff; use それで/それから/あと.
Confusing なお with ただし: なお is not strong enough to set a binding condition.
Confusing it with なおさら (all the more) → different part of speech and meaning.
Omitting the comma after なお makes the sentence hard to read; in JLPT reading questions, the comma helps identify the structure.

rows: Not the conjunction “なお”; different meaning
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>いからなおさら<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたくない。

examples: I agree with his proposal. Mind you, that's only if it can be done within the budget.
I want to study abroad in Japan. That is, if my parents allow it.
This camera performs well. Mind you, it's expensive too.
I think the exam was easy. Whether I passed or not is another matter, though.
I said I wouldn't go. Then again, I might change my mind.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of clause B to correct or supplement clause A.
It does not completely negate A, but softens the statement or adds a condition.
Nuance: Polite and reasoned, somewhat written, as if “making the statement more precise”.
Not strongly emotional like それなのに or それでも; leans toward reasoning and supplementing.

•
Used to add supplementary information, an exception, or to adjust the statement in the preceding clause.

• Close in meaning to “However / Even so / That said…”.
•
Clause B does not completely negate clause A, but only limits it or corrects it to be more precise.

• Often used in written language, mildly formal spoken language, and logical presentation.
fields.notes:
• Appears very often in JLPT reading passages when the author states the main point and then adjusts it with もっとも to be precise or to add an exception.
• Can be translated flexibly: “However”, “That said…”, “Of course…”, “The only thing is…”.
• Usually comes after a period or comma, or can be written as: 「～。 もっとも～。」. explain: Used when supplementing the previous sentence by adding an exception or condition. ⏐ examples: 1. 検査の前夜から飲食禁止です。もっとも水は飲んでもかまいません。
You may not eat or drink from the night before the examination. That said, drinking water is fine.
2. 全員が参加しなければなりません。もっとも病気の場合の別です。
Everyone must participate. That said, cases of illness are an exception.
mistakes: Confusing it with それでも: それでも = doing B anyway even though A is an obstacle; もっとも = only adds an exception or condition.
Using it in strongly emotional contexts such as complaining → unnatural; use それなのに・でも instead.
Omitting clause A: もっとも always builds on preceding information.
Omitting the comma: in written language, write “もっとも、～”。

rows: Adds an exception/condition without completely negating the previous idea.
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>だ。 もっとも、<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いが。
B shows an action/determination that overcomes A.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。 それでも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Disappointment; B strongly contradicts the expectation from A.
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>した。 それなのに<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかった。
Argumentative, strongly negating; used in formal written language.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。 しかし<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかった。

examples: I thought about it from every angle. In short, there's nothing to do but give it a try.
He's busy, and apparently he's not interested either. In short, he isn't coming.
My explanation got long, but in short, this machine can't be used anymore.
You gave all sorts of reasons, but basically, you just don't want to go, right?
This job is difficult and takes time. In short, you need to be prepared for it.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of clause B to draw out the essence/core of clause A.
Nuance: Objective/neutral, or sometimes a little cold and blunt.
Often used when the speaker wants to conclude quickly, or feels the listener is rambling.
Appears often in spoken language, presentations, reports, and JLPT reading tests.

•
Summarizes and concludes the preceding content briefly and concisely.

•
Expresses the main point or essence of a matter after a long or detailed explanation.

•
Natural translations: “In short…”, “In other words…”, “Basically…”, “In the end…”.

• Often used in explanations, presentations, logical conversation, or to emphasize a personal opinion.
fields.notes:
• Usually placed after a period or comma: 「～。 要するに、～。」
• Common in expository texts when the author wants to emphasize the result or the core point.
• Can sound a little sarcastic in conversation: “要するにさ、君はやりたくないんでしょ？” meaning_vi: To put it briefly, in short ～ ⏐ explain: Means explaining the previous sentence in a simple way. ⏐ examples: 1. 試合に大負けした。要するに、相手のチームと力の差があったということだ。
We lost the match badly. In short, there was a gap in ability between us and the other team.
2. 彼は一度も入賞しなかった。要するに、才能がなかったということだ。
He never once won a prize. In short, he had no talent.
mistakes: Confusing it with つまり: つまり = restating information in a different way; 要するに = drawing a conclusion.
Using it when there is no content yet to summarize → unnatural.
Using it in very formal writing such as a thesis → use “結論としては…, 要するに…” or other academic expressions.
Omitting the comma/、 after 要するに in written language is non-standard.

rows: States a brief conclusion after a detailed explanation.
Restates the same information in a different way.
<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>、 つまり、<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>言葉<rt>ことば</rt></ruby>。
Emphasizes the final result after a process.
<ruby>結局<rt>けっきょく</rt></ruby>、<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかった。
More colloquial; close in meaning to <ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに.
<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。

fields.meaning:
～すぎた結果(けっか)→（-）の結果(けっか)
Because of an extreme degree, an excessive result
examples: I was so nervous that I started to feel sick.
My mother worried so much that she fell ill.
In Japan today, there are women who are so concerned about their figure that they go on extreme diets.
In its rush for economic growth, Japan saw environmental destruction advance rapidly.
I was so absorbed in my game that I didn't notice my father had come home.
*It was so cold that I couldn't breathe (= because of the extreme cold, I couldn't breathe).
fields.notes: Attaches to nouns and verbs expressing emotions or states to show that their degree is extreme; the second half describes an undesirable result that happened because of it.
